concepts.guidance: Read as refreshing, salty, bright and sessionable: a long, lime-forward highball or swizzle with ginger or coconut water and a saline edge; nothing heavy or creamy.

concepts.reading: Surfers' dawn patrol: up before sunrise for glassy waves.
concepts.guidance: Read as a bright, low-proof morning drink: coffee-cold-brew highball or a sunrise citrus spritz; light, awake, no cream.

concepts.reading: Duke Kahanamoku (1890–1968): Olympic swimming champion (1912 gold) and the ambassador of surfing.
concepts.guidance: Read as a classic Waikīkī beach-boy drink: clean, athletic, elegant; a light rum and pineapple-lime sour with a sparkling lift.

concepts.reading: The ʻukulele, adapted from the Portuguese machete brought by Madeiran immigrants (1879); popularly 'jumping flea', though Queen Liliʻuokalani glossed it as 'the gift that came here'.
concepts.guidance: Read as small, bright, cheerful and simple: a four-ingredient sour, light rum, lime, a fruity syrup, served up and short.

concepts.reading: The lei: a garland given in welcome, love or farewell, of plumeria, pīkake (jasmine), tuberose, orchid, or the vanilla-scented maile vine.
concepts.guidance: Read as floral and fragrant, a welcome drink: light rum or gin, lime, honey or elderflower, orange-flower water; orchid garnish.

concepts.reading: The Samoan fire-knife dance (siva afi), the climax of Polynesian revues.
concepts.guidance: Read as dramatic and fiery: a flaming garnish (spent lime shell with overproof, lit and extinguished before drinking), ginger and chili warmth, red-gold.

concepts.reading: A request for actual fire. Tiki's flames: overproof in a spent lime shell, a lemon-extract-soaked crouton, a flamed Volcano Bowl crater, cinnamon sparked over the flame. Choose a drink whose structure supports it (zombie, bowl, hot coffee grog) and say to extinguish before drinking. Overproof is for the shell, not more booze in the glass.
Torch- or firelit evenings: smoke and warmth.
concepts.guidance: Read as a smoky-sweet evening drink: Demerara or a touch of mezcal, honey, spice; amber glow; a flame only if asked.

concepts.reading: Mermaids: shimmering, sea-green-blue, pearl and sea-foam. Blue can come from butterfly-pea tea (it shifts violet with citrus, so float it last) or blue curaçao; keep every other ingredient clear so it stays aqua.
concepts.guidance: Read as delicate, saline-kissed and pale aqua: light rum or gin, lime, coconut water, a little lychee or elderflower, a saline drop, a foam 'sea-spray' cap.

concepts.reading: Sirens: luring song, danger under beauty.
concepts.guidance: Shannon Mustipher's Song of the Siren is a catalogue drink; don't reuse that name. Read as seductive and dangerous: floral-fruity on top, a strong dark-rum undertow, a bitter last note.

concepts.reading: Sharks in tiki: Vic's Shark's Tooth, Don's Tiger Shark. Never name it Shark's Tooth, Shark Bite or Tiger Shark (existing drinks).
concepts.guidance: Read as bracing and bitey: overproof Jamaican or Demerara heat, plenty of lime, a red grenadine 'blood' plume; short and sharp.

concepts.reading: Wrecks: storm, salt, timber, survival with the rum casks. (Trader Sam's 'Shipwreck on the Rocks' is bourbon-agave-lemon-mint.)
concepts.guidance: Read as dark, briny, rum-heavy and storm-tossed: navy or Demerara rum, lime, honey, a saline edge, maybe ginger; barrel mug.

concepts.reading: Treasure is gold: aged rum, passion fruit or honey, a little spice, a glow like coins in the lamplight.
Pirates of the golden age (1650–1730) sailed on rum, lime and dark sugar. This one is hearty: Jamaican rum, lime and spice.
concepts.guidance: Avoid bottle-of-rum clichés in the tagline beyond one wink.

concepts.reading: Sea shanties (work songs; 'The Wellerman' went viral in 2021, and its 'sugar and tea and rum' is the spec!). Read literally: rum + tea + sugar, a warm or room-temp navy punch; communal, singing strength.
Reef and lagoon: clear warm water, turquoise shallows, bright fish.
concepts.guidance: Read as light and translucent aqua: white rum, lime, coconut water, a touch of blue curaçao (keep the rest clear), lychee or melon for fish-bright fruit; sea-salt drop.

concepts.reading: The Mai-Kai's Mystery Drink (Fort Lauderdale, 1956–) arrived with a gong and a dancer; Donn Beach coded his recipes (numbered and lettered syrups) so rivals couldn't copy them.
concepts.guidance: Read as a theatrical bowl whose layers are hard to guess: several rums, a coded house mix (Don's Mix, falernum, Pernod drops), served for two or more with ceremony.

concepts.reading: Prohibition rum-running (Rum Row off the US coast; Bill McCoy, popularly but doubtfully the source of 'the real McCoy'); Smuggler's Cove borrowed the mood.
concepts.guidance: Rum Runner is also a 1972 Islamorada resort drink; don't use that name. Read as strong, aged-rum-forward, a bit clandestine: an old-fashioned-shaped rum drink or a dark sour.

concepts.reading: Kava (ʻawa in Hawaiian): a non-alcoholic, earthy, peppery root drink central to ceremony across Fiji, Tonga, Samoa, Vanuatu and Hawaiʻi; numbs the tongue. Vic's 'Kava Bowl' was just a rum punch. Kava itself is not in the vocabulary.
concepts.guidance: Respectfully: don't mimic the ceremony. Read as earthy-peppery and communal: a low-sugar, earthy bowl (agricole or cachaça, a black-pepper/ginger note), or zero-proof if requested.

concepts.reading: Rapa Nui's moai: monumental ancestor figures carved from Rano Raraku tuff, now a favorite tiki mug (popularized by Heyerdahl's Aku-Aku).
concepts.guidance: Respect the ancestors: no head jokes. Read as stoic, monumental, earthy: a strong, stirred or short rum drink with an earthy-smoky edge, served in a Moai mug.

concepts.reading: Polynesian wayfinding: navigating by stars, swells and birds; Hōkūleʻa (1976) proved the voyages.
concepts.guidance: Read as long, steady and ocean-bright: a long swizzle or punch of cane spirit, lime, coconut water, honey; navigational stars in the name, not deities.

concepts.reading: A dragon breathes fire and guards its hoard: smoke, chile heat and a flame at the table.
concepts.guidance: Dragonfly, Golden Dragon and Formidable Dragon are catalogue names; don't reuse.

concepts.reading: Wizards and potions: arcane herbs, bubbling, color change, mystery. Butterbeer (Harry Potter) means butterscotch-cream soda: demerara + butter (hot buttered batter) + vanilla + soda/cream foam. A true color-changing potion: butterfly-pea tea turns violet-pink when the citrus hits it; serve the citrus on the side and let the guest pour.
concepts.guidance: Read as herbal-complex with theater: Chartreuse or Bénédictine with rum, honey, lemon; smoke or a sparkling 'bubbling cauldron' top.

concepts.reading: Unicorns and rainbows: pastel, sparkly, sweet-fruity, whimsical. Never let blue + red mix into gray-purple.
concepts.guidance: Read as a light, pastel-pink fruit punch with sparkle: guava or strawberry pink, lychee/elderflower, sparkling wine; if 'rainbow', layer colors (grenadine sinks, a pale middle, a blue float) and say not to stir.

concepts.reading: Outer space: the 1950s–60s space age gave tiki the Saturn (1967) and the Jet Pilot/Test Pilot naming.
concepts.guidance: Read as cool, dark-sky elegant: a gin or light-rum sour with passion fruit and falernum (Saturn-style), served up; 'galaxy' colors come honestly from butterfly-pea tea, which turns from blue to violet when the citrus goes in: pour it last as a float for the color change; never blue curaçao + grenadine mud.

concepts.reading: Jet- and space-age tiki: Don the Beachcomber's Test Pilot (1941) and Jet Pilot, the Saturn (1967). Never name it Test Pilot, Jet Pilot or Saturn.
concepts.guidance: Read as a precise, strong, spiced Beachcomber sour, crisp and engineered, served in a footed glass.

concepts.reading: Aliens and UFOs: kitsch green, glowing, weird.
concepts.guidance: Read as playful and strange but well made: an herbal-green or melon-green sour (green Chartreuse or melon liqueur with fresh lime and pineapple), maybe a smoky surprise. Green must come from a green ingredient that's actually in it.

concepts.reading: Robots and the future: precision, chrome, clean lines. Cyberpunk adds neon (yuzu, a bright bitter).
concepts.guidance: Read as a clean, precise, minimalist drink: clear or pale, exact proportions (a perfectly balanced Daiquiri-shape), maybe a mechanical metal vessel (julep cup).

concepts.reading: Ghosts: pale, translucent, chilling, an anise whisper.
concepts.guidance: Read as pale and eerie: a clear or white drink (egg-white mist, coconut milk), anise drops, a cold daiquiri shape or a white colada; not the dark Zombie.

concepts.reading: Zombie apocalypse: here the guest is invoking monsters, and tiki has the answer: the Zombie family (Donn Beach, 1934; 'two per customer'). Strong, multi-rum, grapefruit-cinnamon (Don's Mix), Pernod drops, falernum, a 151 float. Name it something new; never 'Zombie'.
Vampires: blood-red, velvet, night, aristocratic. Not a Bloody Mary.
concepts.guidance: Read as deep blood-red and silky: pomegranate/hibiscus or cherry Heering, a dark rum, a bitter-aristocratic edge (Campari or amaro), served up in a coupe.

concepts.reading: Werewolves: wild, forest, smoke, primal.
concepts.guidance: Read as smoky, peppery and feral: rye or mezcal with rum, ginger, a bitter herbal snarl; dark amber.

concepts.reading: Witches and cauldrons: herbal, dark, bubbling, autumnal.
concepts.guidance: Bewitched Blossom is a catalogue name. Read as herbal-dark: amaro or Chartreuse with dark rum, apple or blackberry, spice; a bubbling ginger-beer top for the cauldron.

concepts.reading: The Kraken: Norse sea monster turned black-rum legend.
concepts.guidance: there's also a Kraken black spiced rum brand: don't name it Read as abyssal and ink-dark: black blended rum, molasses, spice, lime, a heavyweight Zombie or grog in a tall glass; a dark float spreading like ink.

concepts.reading: Fairies and enchanted woods: floral, green, delicate, a little mischief.
concepts.guidance: Read as light, floral and herbal: elderflower, mint, cucumber, gin or agricole, honey; pale green only from herbs; flower garnish.
taglineWords: found in a ring of mushrooms

concepts.reading: The phoenix: fire and rebirth, gold-red plumage.
concepts.guidance: Read as a fiery, golden-red bird: passion fruit and grenadine sunrise, ginger heat, a flamed garnish; a nod to the Jungle Bird lineage for 'bird'.

concepts.reading: The yeti: snowy, shaggy, frosty-white.
concepts.guidance: Read as a frosty white frozen drink: coconut, vanilla, a hint of mint or cinnamon, blended snowy, served in a big mug.

concepts.reading: The ghost ship (Flying Dutchman legend): fog, rotting sails, a skeleton crew. Never name it Fog Cutter.
concepts.guidance: Read as foggy and spectral-dark: a Fog Cutter-ish orgeat punch with a dark float, anise mist, or a smoky navy grog.

concepts.reading: The genie and the lamp: spice-market, smoke, gold, wishes.
concepts.guidance: Read as spice-market gold: honey, orange-flower water, cinnamon, a smoke curl; aged rum or brandy; served in a snifter or tulip.

concepts.reading: A trip back in time: 'vintage', 'old school', 'retro'. No blue liqueurs or schnapps.
concepts.guidance: Read as golden-age authenticity: a 1930s–50s Beachcomber or Vic-style recipe with honest ingredients (honey mix, Don's Mix, falernum, orgeat, two or three rums), period glass or mug.

concepts.reading: Superheroes: bold, powerful, colorful, bigger-than-life. Comic/trademark names stay out of the drink name.
concepts.guidance: Read as bold and punchy: a strong, vivid drink with a clear hero flavor (passion fruit or pineapple), high-impact garnish; strength up.

concepts.reading: Greco-Roman sea gods (Poseidon/Neptune, the trident): fair game for a bit of grandeur.
concepts.guidance: Read as regal-oceanic: a three-rum ('trident') grog or swizzle with lime, honey and a saline edge, cold and deep.

concepts.reading: 'For my wine-loving mom': bridge from wine. A tiki cobbler or a sherry-touched punch, not a sugar bomb. Without 'wine', 'mom' alone shouldn't force anything.
concepts.guidance: Use fortified and aromatized wines (Lillet, amontillado, sweet vermouth, port) or a sparkling-wine crown, lighter rum or brandy, fresh citrus and fruit; low to moderate proof, elegant glass (coupe, flute, tulip).

concepts.reading: A wine drinker: values acidity, dryness, aromatics, food-friendliness.
concepts.guidance: Use wine and fortified wine as modifiers (sherry, Lillet, port, vermouth, sparkling), dry citrus balance, moderate proof; a punch or cobbler.

concepts.reading: Our grandparents' tiki was the mid-century kind, Trader Vic's and Don's, brandy and rum and never neon. This one is gentle and familiar.
concepts.guidance: Respect: age doesn't mean sweet; let other words lead.
taglineWords: the way they poured it in '58

concepts.reading: A tiki newcomer: start with an approachable icon structure (Mai Tai-, Daiquiri- or Painkiller-shaped), recognisable flavors (lime, pineapple, orange, almond, coconut), one or two rums, moderate strength, no overproof bite or absinthe rinse, a fun garnish. Explain the family lineage so they learn. (Malihini = newcomer in Hawaiian.)

A whiskey drinker: give them tiki through their spirit. Precedents: Vic's Honi Honi (bourbon Mai Tai), the Port Light (bourbon, passion fruit, lemon), the Eastern Sour, the Paniolo Old Fashioned. Bourbon or rye as base, a tropical modifier (falernum, allspice, passion fruit, orgeat), spirit-forward balance.
taglineWords: for the whiskey side of the bar

concepts.reading: Someone who hates rum: tiki without rum has deep precedent: gin (Saturn, Vic's gin drinks), bourbon (Honi Honi, Port Light), brandy (Scorpion components), tequila/mezcal (craft-era riffs), aquavit, pisco.
concepts.guidance: Exclude every rum and rum-based liqueur (coconut rum, spiced rum, Swedish punsch); keep tiki modifiers.

concepts.reading: A gin drinker: botanicals and dryness. Tiki-gin precedents: the Saturn (1967), Vic's Fog Cutter/Scorpion (gin in support), the Singapore Sling, Suffering Bastard. Gin base, passion fruit/falernum/orgeat, lemon, crisp; or a gin swizzle.
taglineWords: for the gin side of the bar

concepts.reading: An agave lover: tequila or mezcal in tiki skeletons is well established in the craft era (Tiki Margaritas, mezcal Mai Tais, Pirate King Punch's tequila base). Agave base, lime, passion fruit/pineapple, falernum or orgeat, chili optional; salt welcome.
A vodka drinker likes clean, neutral, uncomplicated. Tiki precedent: the Chi Chi (vodka colada) and Harry Yee's Blue Hawaii (vodka + rum).
concepts.guidance: Use vodka as base (or white rum as a gentle step), fresh fruit, crisp citrus, low funk; no overproof.

concepts.reading: A beer drinker: long, refreshing, bitter-edged, effervescent. Ginger beer bucks and grog-with-soda are the bridge (beer itself is a missing ingredient: a tiki shandy would need lager). Long, dry-ish, bitter hint, fizzy; not creamy.

For a bartender: they want something they haven't had, made with care: unusual but logical (bitter, agricole, aquavit, Batavia arrack, sherry), restrained sweetness, technique respected, a nod to a deep-cut precedent. Fernet or amaro has industry-handshake status. Not sweet, not gimmicky.
taglineWords: for the other side of the bar

concepts.reading: A tiki aficionado (Beachbum Berry / Smuggler's Cove literate): blended rums by category (Cate's taxonomy), Donn Beach seasoning (Don's Mix, falernum, Pernod drops, Angostura), fresh juice, correct dilution and ice, a period-correct vessel. Deep-cut riff with lineage; never blue liqueurs, sour mix or coconut rum.

To impress: theatre plus quality. A flaming spent-lime shell or Volcano Bowl, a striking vessel (Scorpion bowl, pineapple, skull), a layered float, a dramatic garnish (orchid + mint bouquet + cherry); but the recipe must still be balanced, and makeable at home (no rare ingredients).

phrases: not a fan of strong drinks
concepts.reading: For someone who likes sweet drinks or dislikes the taste of alcohol: lower proof, more juice and creaminess, softer rums (light, Barbados), fruit-forward (pineapple, passion fruit, coconut, banana), still balanced with acid. Be honest in the explanation that strength hides well in juicy drinks.
The designated driver deserves a real tiki drink, not a glass of juice: spiced syrups, fresh citrus, a tea or ginger backbone and the full garnish ceremony, with no alcohol at all.
taglineWords: all of the ceremony, none of the proof

concepts.reading: A bitter lover: the Jungle Bird lineage (Campari + dark rum + pineapple), Trinidad Sour (Angostura as base), Kingston Negroni, amaro-tiki. Bitter tiki family, low sugar, rich rum.
A coffee lover: Coffee Grog and Kona traditions; coffee as a real component (cold brew or espresso, coffee liqueur), aged rum, warm spice, low acid. Hot or cold.

A culinary audience: savory-leaning balance, interesting texture, salt as seasoning, food-friendly acidity and moderate sugar. Saline, sherry, herbs (basil, cucumber), fresh ginger; a sour or swizzle that pairs with food.

Lower-sugar request: cut syrups and liqueurs, lean on fresh citrus, soda/coconut water length, aromatics (mint, ginger, bitters) and a smaller pour; avoid cream of coconut and nectar. Be honest: alcohol has calories too.
A date night wants something elegant and easy to talk over, at a gentle strength.
concepts.guidance: For a partner or date: don't stereotype by gender ('for my girlfriend' does not mean pink and sweet; 'for my husband' does not mean whiskey).

concepts.reading: A crowd wants one big bowl, built so everyone can have a second cup.
concepts.guidance: Avoid divisive ingredients (absinthe rinse, Islay, heavy bitter).

concepts.reading: Sophisticated and safe: polished, not kitschy; a clear, elegant, balanced drink in a coupe or rocks glass; moderate strength, low novelty, quality aged rum or a refined gin sour.
concepts.guidance: Garnish restrained (a twist, an orchid at most).

concepts.reading: Budget/college: common, cheap bottles only (cost 1), few ingredients, batchable, fun; never compromise fresh lime. Moderate proof (responsibility).

A Scotch drinker: smoke and malt. Tiki precedents use Scotch sparingly (Islay floats on a Penicillin-like tiki sour, Scotch in Vic-era 'Mai Tai' variants is rare). Blended Scotch base with honey, ginger, lemon; an Islay float; maybe falernum.
A brandy drinker: Trader Vic loved brandy (Scorpion, Fog Cutter). Brandy base or co-base with rum, orgeat, orange, lemon, a sherry float: the orgeat-punch family.

Someone who wants real heat: chili (Ancho Reyes, fresh jalapeño), fresh ginger, black pepper; balanced with fruit (pineapple, mango, passion fruit) and lime so it's not just burn. Tell them the heat level.

Silky: rounded mouthfeel without being thick. Achieved with egg white (shaken dry first), a little coconut milk, orgeat or honey, gum/pineapple syrup, Velvet falernum, and less sharp acid; aged rum over overproof. Not necessarily creamy-opaque.
Velvety: richer than silky: cream of coconut, cream, egg, PX sherry or butter batter, aged and dark rums, warm spice. Dense but still balanced.

Fizzy: carbonation is the texture. Top (never shake) with soda, ginger beer, tonic or sparkling wine; build tall over ice; keep the shaken base slightly over-concentrated to survive the top. A Grog with soda, a Swizzle with a sparkling crown, or a Buck.

Frosty: the glass frosts and the drink runs very cold: swizzled on crushed ice in a metal cup or collins (Queen's Park Swizzle, julep), or flash-blended/frozen. Mint and cooling flavors help; keep sugar a touch higher since cold dulls sweetness.
Frozen is the blender's art: ice whirled to a sorbet, sweeter and fruitier than a shaken drink, because cold mutes both.

Fiery: actual heat. Chili (Ancho Reyes, muddled jalapeño), fresh ginger, black pepper/five-spice, cinnamon; balance with sugar, fruit and lime so heat reads as pleasant. Not to be confused with 'warming' (spice/boozy) or 'hot' (temperature).
A cold night wants warmth: baking spice, a dark spirit and a little heat.
Bracing: high acid and dryness with a clean finish: extra lime/grapefruit, less sugar, a dry rum or agricole, bitters; served very cold, short. Daiquiri/Grog territory.
Refreshing means long, cold and bright, lightly sweet, with something aromatic like mint or ginger.

Boozy/spirit-forward: more spirit, less juice; stirred or a short sour with an overproof component kept to the dose classics use (¾–1 oz 151). Zombie and stirred families. Warn about strength in the explanation.
Light: low proof, low body, high aromatics: white rum or agricole, bright citrus, soda or coconut water, a floral/herbal touch; no dairy or dark rum.
Dessert-like: creamy or rich, sweeter, low acid, warm notes (vanilla, chocolate, caramel, coffee, banana, coconut). Colada or stirred/flip structures, smaller pour.
Frothy: a foam cap from egg white (dry shake), aquafaba, or a hard-shaken pineapple juice (pineapple foams naturally) or flash-blend; a sour structure, served up or in a pilsner.
Smooth: no harsh edges: aged/column rums rather than overproof or funky pot still, enough sugar and dilution, rounded modifiers (orgeat, honey, vanilla). Moderate proof.
Dry: minimal residual sugar; push acid-to-sugar ratio toward a Daiquiri's 8:1 or drier, use dry modifiers (dry curaçao, amontillado, dry vermouth, bitters), avoid nectars and cream of coconut.
Juicy: fruit-forward, mouth-filling: real juices and nectars (pineapple, passion fruit, mango, guava, orange), longer build, moderate proof; resort punch or Punch family.
Minty-cool: lots of fresh mint (spanked, not shredded), crushed ice, lime; a Swizzle (Queen's Park) or Julep-cup build; optionally a Fernet/Chartreuse accent. Pale green only from mint itself.
Salty/briny: a saline solution (a few drops, not a rim's worth) lifts fruit and dulls bitterness; amontillado and Islay bring brine; li hing mui is salty-sweet-sour.
concepts.guidance: Keep it seasoning, not soup.
taglineWords: with a pinch of sea salt

concepts.reading: Bittersweet: sugar and bitterness held in tension: Campari/Aperol/amaro with pineapple and dark rum (Jungle Bird), or Angostura-forward.

Tingly/numbing: Sichuan peppercorn or buzz-button (spilanthes) flowers make the mouth buzz; neither is in the vocabulary (missing). Approximate with five-spice syrup (contains Sichuan pepper), fresh ginger and effervescence; say it's an approximation.
Full-bodied: dark and Demerara rums, rich syrups (demerara 2:1), PX or cream of coconut, honey/butter; heavier pour; colada or stirred.

A stronger drink (not 'the strongest'): raise spirit share within the family's ABV band, trim juice and lengtheners, add a measured overproof component (¼–½ oz) rather than doubling everything; keep balance by trimming sugar proportionally.
Low proof is built for several rounds: a long drink on wine, sherry or bubbles with bright citrus, around seven percent.

Sweeter: raise sugar a notch within the family window (toward ~12–14:1 sugar:acid), prefer flavorful sweeteners (honey, demerara, fruit syrups, cream of coconut) over plain syrup; never drop acid to zero.
Tarter: push toward the Daiquiri's ~8:1 sugar:acid; add lime or grapefruit, cut nectars; keep a little sugar so it doesn't taste thin.

Complex: Donn Beach's method: two or three rums by category, a secret seasoning (Don's Mix, falernum, allspice, Pernod drops, Angostura), two citruses, a fruit and a spice syrup; or a bitter/fortified component. Complexity must be legible: each component has a job.
Simple means three to five bottles from any good shop, and syrups you can stir up in a minute.
taglineWords: from what's already in the cupboard

concepts.reading: Balanced: aim for the family's median chemistry exactly (ABV, sugar, acid), no extremes, no flavor dominating; it's the default, so mostly a request to avoid gimmicks.

Classic-style: golden-age (1934–1960s) technique and pantry: fresh lime and grapefruit, honey mix, Don's Mix, falernum, orgeat, curaçao, two or three rums by category, crushed ice, flash blend; Don's or Vic's structures. No blue liqueur, schnapps, sour mix or coconut rum.

Modern/craft: revival-era balance (fresh, strong, measured), inversions and unusual bases (Angostura as base, Chartreuse, mezcal, aquavit, sherry), bitter elements, precise garnish; clean presentation over kitsch.

Crowd-pleaser: the famous-drink profile from the catalogue (longer, gentler ~12% ABV, slightly sweeter, five ingredients): pineapple, lime, orange, almond or coconut, two familiar rums; no divisive bitters, smoke or anise.
Hangover: tiki has the canonical cure, Joe Scialom's Suffering Bastard (Shepheard's Hotel, Cairo, 1942): gin, brandy, lime, Angostura, ginger beer.
concepts.guidance: Don't reuse 'Suffering Bastard'; 'Corpse Reviver' is a classic name too. Read as a ginger-beer buck: hydrating, gingery, bitters, lower proof, maybe a coffee or coconut-water element.

concepts.reading: Pretty means color from real ingredients and a glass that shows it off.
Huge: volume, not necessarily proof. A bowl (Scorpion, Tiki Bowl) or a 20 oz hurricane/pineapple with juice and lengtheners; keep ABV moderate.
Small: 3–4 oz finished, served up (Nick & Nora, coupe) or short on a cube; concentrated flavor; a Daiquiri or stirred structure.
Over-the-top: maximal tiki theatre (a garnish bouquet, flaming shell, float, special vessel), up to Zombie-level complexity, still balanced. Pair complexity with a theatrical vessel.
Minimalist: three or four ingredients, one rum, a single precise garnish, served up or on one cube: Daiquiri, Ti' Punch or a stirred rum drink. The rum should be good enough to carry it.

Rum-forward: high spirit share, characterful rums (Jamaican pot still, Demerara, agricole, aged Barbados), little juice; Daiquiri, Ti' Punch, rum Old Fashioned, Mai Tai (which was built to show off rum).
No/low citrus: build balance from other levers: stirred structures (bitters, fortified wine), creamy coladas (fat balances sugar), tea or coffee lengtheners, pineapple's gentle acid only if allowed.
concepts.guidance: Exclude lime, lemon, grapefruit, yuzu, lime cordial, Don's Mix.

concepts.reading: A signature drink for an event: batchable, crowd-pleasing, photogenic, moderate proof, a story in the name (use the couple's or event's imagery, not a classic's name); bowl or pre-batched service.
Fast/no equipment: built in the glass over ice (a highball, buck or punch), or stirred in a mixing glass; no egg white, no blending, no homemade syrup.

Dragon fruit (pitaya): mild kiwi-melon flavor with a startling magenta flesh (red pitaya). The color is the point; the flavor is gentle, so support it with lime, lychee or passion fruit and a light rum or agricole. Pink comes from the fruit, not from grenadine.

Jamaica gave the world high-ester pot-still rum (Hampden, Worthy Park, Appleton, Wray & Nephew overproof), the Planter's Punch and pimento, the berry behind allspice dram. Ginger and Ting, the island's grapefruit soda, were everyday flavors long before tiki. So this one is funky Jamaican rum and lime, with allspice and grapefruit soda.
Jamaica's Blue Mountain coffee: a coffee-and-rum drink with dark Jamaican rum and a touch of allspice. 'Blue' here is a mountain range, not a color, so no blue curaçao.

Barbados is round, vanilla-and-banana blended pot/column rum (Mount Gay since 1703, Foursquare), the rum-punch rhyme, and falernum, which is Barbadian; John D. Taylor's Velvet Falernum comes from there. Corn 'n' Oil (Bajan rum and falernum with bitters) and a nutmeg-dusted rum punch are the local signatures.

Crop Over is Barbados's festival marking the end of the sugar-cane harvest (it peaks with Grand Kadooment in early August). It calls for a festive Bajan rum punch: Barbados rum, falernum, lime and bitters, long and cold.
taglineWords: for the end of the cane harvest

concepts.reading: Martinique is rhum agricole: fresh cane-juice rum under its own AOC (1996), grassy and peppery when white, dry and spicy when aged. The local ritual is the Ti' Punch (white rhum, a lime coin and cane syrup, 'chacun prépare sa propre mort': each makes their own). The Planteur is the longer, juice-and-spice version.
concepts.guidance: Keep it lean and rhum-forward.
taglineWords: the Martinique way: each makes their own

concepts.reading: Guadeloupe and Marie-Galante make both cane-juice rhum (white rhums often bottled at 50–59%) and molasses rum. The Christmas liqueur shrubb is rum steeped with orange peel and spice.
concepts.guidance: Read it as agricole with orange peel, cinnamon and a Planteur-style splash of fruit.
taglineWords: with a twist of Guadeloupe orange peel

concepts.reading: Haiti means Barbancourt (cane-juice rum, double-distilled, vanilla and soft grass) and clairin, the wild, terroir-driven cane spirit of small village stills. Don the Beachcomber's Port au Prince took its name from the capital.
concepts.guidance: Read it as grassy-vanilla rum with lime and warm spice, and coconut for the holiday side (kremas).

concepts.reading: The Caribbean's holiday nogs: Puerto Rican coquito (coconut milk, cream of coconut, rum, cinnamon, nutmeg, vanilla), Haitian kremas (the same idea with warm spice and a little lime zest) and Trinidad's ponche de crème (milk, egg, rum, Angostura and nutmeg). They are creamy, spiced, citrus-free and served cold in small glasses. This is a coconut nog, not a colada, so no pineapple.
Caribbean Christmas sorrel is hibiscus (roselle) steeped with ginger, pimento and clove, sweetened and spiked with overproof rum. It is deep ruby, tart and gingery.
concepts.guidance: Read it as hibiscus, ginger and allspice, with a Jamaican overproof kick.

concepts.reading: Trinidad is the home of Angostura bitters (made in Port of Spain) and of the Queen's Park Swizzle (Queen's Park Hotel, 1920s): Demerara or aged rum, lime, sugar and mint, swizzled, with a crown of bitters. The Trinidad Sour turned 1½ oz of Angostura into the base.
concepts.guidance: Read it as bitters-forward, swizzled and minty.
taglineWords: swizzled the Port of Spain way

concepts.reading: Havana is precision with light rum: Constantino Ribalaigua's Floridita Daiquiris (lime, sugar, maraschino or grapefruit; the frappé blended style), the Mojito, El Presidente and the Hotel Nacional. American visitors drank there during Prohibition, and Donn Beach and Trader Vic both learned from it.
concepts.guidance: Read it as crisp, lime-forward and spare.
taglineWords: the way Constante shook them in Havana

concepts.reading: Havana in the 1950s danced at the Tropicana and drank at El Floridita, where the Daiquiri No. 4 came blended to snow with maraschino, and at the Hotel Nacional, whose Special married rum, pineapple and apricot. Glamour over grit.
taglineWords: for a Havana night at the cabaret

concepts.reading: Puerto Rico is light column rum (Don Q, Bacardí at Cataño) and the Piña Colada: credited to Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero at the Caribe Hilton in 1954, though Barrachina in Old San Juan claims 1963. Coco López cream of coconut made it possible. A Puerto Rican prayer should taste of pineapple and coconut, or of parcha (passion fruit), over light rum.

The Dominican Republic makes dry, light-bodied aged column rums (Brugal, Barceló). Its folk drink, mamajuana, is rum, red wine and honey steeped on bark and herbs. Passion fruit (chinola) is everywhere.
concepts.guidance: Read it as dry aged rum with honey, a little wine-dark fruit and chinola.

concepts.reading: Guyana's Demerara rums come from the Diamond distillery and its heritage wooden stills (Port Mourant double wooden pot, Enmore wooden Coffey, Versailles). They taste of burnt sugar, smoke and dried fruit. They are the backbone of navy rum, the Navy Grog and the Zombie's 151.
concepts.guidance: Read it as dark, rich and smoky, with honey and grapefruit to cut it.

concepts.reading: Bermuda is Gosling's black rum, the Dark 'n Stormy (black rum over ginger beer with lime) and the Bermuda Rum Swizzle (black and gold rum, pineapple, orange, falernum, grenadine and bitters, swizzled).
concepts.guidance: Read it as molasses-black rum with ginger, built long.
taglineWords: with a Bermuda squall in it

concepts.reading: The Bahamas gave the resort era the Bahama Mama and the Goombay Smash (Miss Emily's Blue Bee Bar, Green Turtle Cay: coconut rum, dark rum and pineapple). The local Sky Juice is gin, coconut water, condensed milk and nutmeg.
concepts.guidance: Read it as coconut and pineapple, bright and festive like Junkanoo.

concepts.reading: The BVI are Painkiller country: the drink came from the Soggy Dollar Bar on Jost Van Dyke, where guests swim ashore and pay with wet money. Pusser's navy rum goes over pineapple, orange and cream of coconut, with a heap of nutmeg. St. Croix adds Cruzan light rums.
concepts.guidance: Read it as navy rum, coconut, pineapple, orange and nutmeg.

concepts.reading: Curaçao the island gave curaçao the liqueur, made from the peel of the bitter Laraha orange. Aruba and Bonaire are dry, windy desert islands with resort bars (the Aruba Ariba: rum, vodka, banana and fruit juices). The blue version is a choice, not the default.
concepts.guidance: Read it as orange liqueur, light rum and fresh orange.

concepts.reading: Grenada, the 'Spice Isle', grows nutmeg (it is on the national flag), mace, cinnamon, clove and cacao. Its Rivers rum is cane-juice pot-still rum from a water-wheel distillery; Clarke's Court and Westerhall are the others. A Grenadian rum punch is buried in fresh nutmeg. (Grenada is not grenadine, which is named for the pomegranate.)
taglineWords: with a whole Spice Isle of nutmeg

concepts.reading: St. Lucia Distillers blend pot and column rums (Chairman's Reserve). The island grows bananas and cacao and sits under the twin Pitons.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a rounded rum punch with banana, a touch of cacao and Caribbean spice.

concepts.reading: The generic Caribbean prayer is the island rum punch: one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak, with Angostura and fresh nutmeg, often reddened with grenadine and a splash of juice. Lime, aged rum, bitters and nutmeg are the minimum.
concepts.guidance: Use real Caribbean rum styles, not novelty liqueurs.

concepts.reading: Mainland Latin America makes aged column rums (Flor de Caña in Nicaragua, Zacapa in Guatemala, Diplomático and Santa Teresa in Venezuela, Dictador and Ron Medellín in Colombia), some of them noticeably sweetened, plus coffee and maracuyá (passion fruit). Note that some Spanish-style aged rums carry added sugar.
concepts.guidance: Read it as oaky, caramel aged rum with passion fruit or coffee and a lime edge.

concepts.reading: Colonial New England distilled molasses rum (Medford rum was famous) and drank punch. Philadelphia's Fish House Punch (1732) is rum, Cognac, peach brandy, lemon and tea, and the region adds cranberry, maple and apple.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a rum-and-brandy punch with lemon, peach and tea, meant for a bowl.

concepts.reading: Real Hawaiian flavors are lilikoʻi (passion fruit), guava, pineapple, POG (passion-orange-guava juice), li hing mui (salted plum, from Chinese crack-seed shops), coconut and Kona coffee. The resort canon is the Royal Hawaiian Mai Tai (Vic, 1953, with pineapple) and Harry Yee's Blue Hawaii (1957).
concepts.guidance: Read it as passion fruit, guava and pineapple over gold rum, not as blue liqueur by default.
taglineWords: with lilikoʻi and guava, Hawaiian style

concepts.reading: Kona, on the Big Island, grows Hawaii's famous coffee on volcanic slopes, and macadamia orchards are nearby.
concepts.guidance: Read it as coffee and dark rum with a nutty note (orgeat stands in for macadamia) and a little vanilla: a Kona coffee grog, hot or iced.
taglineWords: from the coffee slopes above Kona

concepts.reading: Tahiti gave the Mai Tai its name: Trader Vic's Tahitian friends said 'maita'i roa ae', 'out of this world, the best'. The island's signatures were always vanilla and the tiare, its own gardenia. So this is a Mai Tai with Tahitian vanilla, crowned with a tiare.
taglineWords: with a tiare tucked behind the ear

concepts.reading: The 'South Seas' of tiki are a Hollywood fantasy built on Caribbean rum drinks. The decor is Polynesian; the drinks are Don and Vic's: layered rums, lime, passion fruit, falernum and orgeat, with real island produce (coconut, pineapple, vanilla).
concepts.guidance: Read it as a classic tiki sour, and borrow real Pacific ingredients rather than caricature.
taglineWords: from somewhere south of the equator

concepts.reading: Fiji grows sugar cane and makes its own molasses rum. It is also ginger, coconut, papaya (pawpaw), mango and lime country, and the Coral Coast runs along Viti Levu. Kava (yaqona) is ceremonial and non-alcoholic, so leave it out of a cocktail.
concepts.guidance: Read it as papaya, coconut water, ginger and lime over gold rum.

concepts.reading: Samoa is coconut cream (pe'epe'e), koko Samoa (a roasted-cacao drink), papaya and taro. In tiki it means Trader Vic's Samoan Fog Cutter (rum, brandy, gin, lemon, orange, orgeat, sherry float) and the Samoan Typhoon.
concepts.guidance: Read it as an orgeat punch with a cacao-coconut side note.

concepts.reading: Captain Cook called Tonga the 'Friendly Islands'. Tiki borrowed the name for San Francisco's Tonga Room (1945, with an indoor rainstorm) and Trader Vic's Tonga Punch (rum, orange, curaçao, grenadine, lemon and lime). Tonga grows vanilla (Vava'u) and watermelon.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a bright orange-citrus rum punch.

concepts.reading: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) gave tiki the moai mug. The island is Chilean, so pisco is the local spirit, and Rapa Nui grows pineapple.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a pisco-and-pineapple sour served in a moai mug.
taglineWords: under the gaze of the moai

concepts.reading: Australia has Queensland molasses rum (Bundaberg), passionfruit on everything, and 'lemon, lime and bitters' (a long soft drink heavy on Angostura).
concepts.guidance: Read it as passion fruit and lime, with bitters and ginger beer, built long.

concepts.reading: Filipino bartenders built tiki. Ray Buhen (Tiki-Ti) and Mariano Licudine (Mai-Kai) came up behind Don the Beachcomber's bar. The islands give calamansi (a lime-mandarin citrus; use lime with a little yuzu or orange), Carabao mango, buko (young coconut) and Tanduay rum. Tiki's Lapu Lapu, named for the hero of Mactan, is served in a hollowed pineapple (Disney's Polynesian Village made it famous).
concepts.guidance: Read it as mango, calamansi and coconut over gold rum.
taglineWords: for the Filipino bartenders who built tiki

concepts.reading: Java made Batavia arrack, the funky, tea-like sugarcane-and-red-rice spirit behind the first punches and Swedish punsch. The Moluccas, the original Spice Islands, are the home of clove and nutmeg.
concepts.guidance: Read it as arrack punch: arrack, citrus, tea, demerara sugar and clove-nutmeg spice.

concepts.reading: Bali is frangipani, coconut, ginger, lemongrass and pandan, with arak (palm or rice spirit) as the local pour. Batavia arrack is the safe, regulated stand-in.
concepts.guidance: Lemongrass and pandan would be truer if they were in the pantry. Read it as coconut water, ginger, lime and a floral note over arrack and light rum.

concepts.reading: Malaysia is the birthplace of the Jungle Bird (Jeffrey Ong, Aviary Bar, Kuala Lumpur Hilton, 1973): dark rum, Campari, pineapple, lime and demerara.
concepts.guidance: The local pantry adds gula melaka (palm sugar) and pandan. Read it as bitter tiki with pineapple.
taglineWords: from the Aviary Bar’s long shadow

concepts.reading: Singapore means the Singapore Sling (Raffles Hotel, c. 1915, attributed to Ngiam Tong Boon): gin, cherry liqueur, Bénédictine and citrus. The modern Raffles version is pink with pineapple and grenadine.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a long gin sling with cherry, herbal Bénédictine, pineapple and lime.
taglineWords: for a slow ceiling-fan afternoon in the Straits

concepts.reading: Thai flavor is lime, chili, coconut, lemongrass, Thai basil, galangal and palm sugar. The local spirits are molasses based (Mekhong is mostly molasses with some rice; SangSom is a rum).
concepts.guidance: With this pantry: basil, chili, ginger, lime and coconut over gold rum, balancing sour, sweet, salty and hot the way a Thai cook would.

concepts.reading: Thai iced tea (cha yen) is strong black tea, often with star anise and vanilla, sweetened and topped with condensed and evaporated milk. Its orange color comes from food dye, so a natural version is tan.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a tea-and-cream rum punch with no citrus, because acid curdles the milk.

concepts.reading: Vietnam's signature drink is cà phê sữa đá: strong dark-roast coffee dripped through a phin over sweetened condensed milk and ice. No citrus.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a creamy coffee-and-dark-rum drink, a touch of salt optional (salt coffee is a Hué specialty).
taglineWords: dripped slow like a Saigon phin

concepts.reading: Cantonese cooking and tiki grew up together: Trader Vic's and Don the Beachcomber served Cantonese food, and many Polynesian palaces had Chinese-American owners and cooks. The flavors are lychee, ginger, five-spice, salted plum (li hing) and black tea.
concepts.guidance: Read it as lychee and ginger over light rum, with a five-spice or tea note.

concepts.reading: Tokyo's Ginza bars became famous for precision: exact measures, clear ice, a whisky highball poured just so. This one carries Japanese whisky and yuzu.
concepts.guidance: Shiso, matcha and umeshu would be truer still but aren't stocked.

concepts.reading: Okinawa is Japan's tropical south: awamori (a rice spirit), shikuwasa citrus, kokutō black sugar, Nago pineapple and jasmine tea (sanpin-cha).
concepts.guidance: awamori is not in the pantry Read it as dark-sugar, citrus-bright and gently floral. Use yuzu for shikuwasa, demerara syrup for kokutō, and light rum for awamori.

concepts.reading: India is punch's first home: the earliest English mention (1632) comes from an East India Company man, and the word is usually traced to Hindi 'panch', five. Masala chai spices (ginger, clove, cinnamon, black pepper, cardamom), Alphonso mango and the vanilla-dark Old Monk rum are the modern signatures.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a tea-and-spice rum punch.

concepts.reading: Goa's spirit is feni, distilled from cashew apple or coconut sap and often drunk with lime and a lemon-lime soda.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a beach-shack highball: an unaged fruity spirit (pisco is the nearest stand-in) with lime, soda, coconut water and a pinch of salt.

concepts.reading: Sri Lanka makes coconut arrack (distilled from coconut-flower sap), Ceylon tea and true Ceylon cinnamon. Batavia arrack stands in for the coconut arrack.
concepts.guidance: Read it as an arrack-and-tea punch with cinnamon and lime.

concepts.reading: Réunion (once Île Bourbon, hence 'Bourbon vanilla'), Mauritius and Madagascar are vanilla, lychee and pink-peppercorn country, and their house drink is rhum arrangé: rum steeped with fruit, vanilla and spice. Zanzibar is clove.
concepts.guidance: Read it as vanilla-and-lychee over rhum, lightly spiced.

concepts.reading: Mexico is tequila and mezcal, lime, agave, chili-salt and grapefruit (the Paloma, the clay-pot Cantarito of Jalisco). Tepache (fermented pineapple with piloncillo and cinnamon) and hibiscus (jamaica) are street flavors.
concepts.guidance: Read it as agave-forward with lime and grapefruit, and Trader Vic's agave Mai Tai shape (the Pinky Gonzales) is fair game.

concepts.reading: Oaxaca is mezcal country: agave roasted in earthen pits (palenques), served neat with orange slices and sal de gusano. Phil Ward's Oaxaca Old Fashioned (reposado, mezcal, agave, mole bitters) and Ivy Mix's Tia Mia (mezcal plus Jamaican rum in a Mai Tai) are the craft bridges.
concepts.guidance: The local pantry adds mole, chocolate and chiles. Read it as smoke, agave, orange and cacao.
taglineWords: with the smoke of an Oaxacan palenque

concepts.reading: In Mexico 'jamaica' means hibiscus: agua de jamaica is a tart, cranberry-like, deep-ruby infusion. This is about the flower, not the island.
concepts.guidance: Read it as hibiscus with lime, over tequila or light rum, with a whisper of cinnamon.

concepts.reading: The Yucatán is cenotes, sour orange (naranja agria), habanero and Xtabentún, a Mayan anise-and-honey liqueur.
concepts.guidance: Read it as honey and a whisper of anise, orange-and-lime sourness and a little chili heat over tequila or light rum, cool as a cenote.

concepts.reading: Acapulco and the Mexican Pacific riviera were the 1950s–60s jet set's playground (cliff divers at La Quebrada).
concepts.guidance: Read it as a resort sour: tequila or light rum, pineapple and grapefruit, orange liqueur and lime, with a little coconut.

concepts.reading: Brazil is cachaça (fresh cane-juice spirit), the Caipirinha (lime muddled with sugar) and the batida (cachaça shaken with coconut milk or passion fruit; Bahia does them best).
concepts.guidance: Read it as cachaça and muddled lime, with maracujá (passion fruit) or coconut for the batida side.

concepts.reading: Peru is pisco (Quebranta, Italia, Acholado grapes). Its classics are the Pisco Sour (lime, sugar, egg white, Amargo or Angostura bitters on the foam; usually credited to Victor Morris's bar in Lima, 1920s) and the Chilcano (pisco, lime and ginger ale). Chile also claims pisco.
concepts.guidance: Chicha morada (purple corn) and lúcuma are local but not in the pantry. Read it as pisco, lime and egg-white foam, or pisco and ginger built long.
taglineWords: from the pisco valleys of Ica

concepts.reading: New Orleans gives tiki the Hurricane (Pat O'Brien's, 1940s: dark rum, lemon and passion-fruit syrup), Peychaud's bitters and Herbsaint (anise), and Beachbum Berry's Latitude 29 (2014).
concepts.guidance: Read it as passion fruit and dark rum, with anise and Peychaud's as seasoning.
taglineWords: for a second line down Frenchmen Street

concepts.reading: Miami is Cuban exile culture (the Mojito, café cubano, guava pastelitos) laid over pastel Art Deco, plus the 1980s Miami Vice: a piña colada and a strawberry daiquiri poured side by side in one glass.
concepts.guidance: Read it as light rum, lime and mint, with guava and pastel pink as the accents.

concepts.reading: The Keys mean Key limes (small, aromatic, more bitter), Hemingway's Key West years, sunset at Mallory Square, and the Rum Runner (Holiday Isle Tiki Bar, Islamorada, 1972: rum, banana, blackberry, grenadine and lime). Prohibition rum-running from Cuba and the Bahamas passed through.
concepts.guidance: Read it as lime-sharp, with banana and blackberry for the Rum Runner side.

concepts.reading: Florida is Indian River grapefruit and oranges, plus a deep tiki history: Fort Lauderdale's Mai-Kai (opened 1956, run behind the bar by ex-Beachcomber Mariano Licudine) kept Don's recipes alive for decades.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a Beachcomber-style sour with fresh grapefruit and orange, honey and falernum.

concepts.reading: Hollywood is where tiki began: Donn Beach's bar on McCadden Place (1933/34), the Zombie (1934), and then the Tiki-Ti on Sunset (1961, Ray Buhen), the Luau and the Tonga Hut.
concepts.guidance: Read it as Don's house style: two or three rums, lime and grapefruit, Don's Mix (grapefruit-cinnamon), falernum and honey, drops of anise and bitters.
taglineWords: in the dim light of a Hollywood rum den

concepts.reading: The Bay Area is Trader Vic's country: Hinky Dink's in Oakland became Trader Vic's in 1937, and the Mai Tai followed in 1944, along with the Scorpion and Fog Cutter. The Tonga Room (1945), the Pisco Punch (Bank Exchange, 1890s), Smuggler's Cove (2009) and the Chartreuse Swizzle (2003) are local too.
concepts.guidance: Read it as orgeat, curaçao, lime and aged rum, or Vic's brandy-and-gin orgeat punches.
taglineWords: with the Bay’s fog rolling in

concepts.reading: Palm Springs is mid-century desert modernism, Rat Pack poolside cocktails and a deep tiki streak: Don the Beachcomber had a Palm Springs branch, the Caliente Tropics motel survives, and the revival brought Bootlegger Tiki and a Tonga Hut. Coachella Valley grows dates (the date shake) and grapefruit.
concepts.guidance: Read it as grapefruit-bright, poolside and lightly date-rich.
taglineWords: poolside under the San Jacinto range

concepts.reading: Las Vegas tiki was showbiz: the Aku Aku at the Stardust (1960), flaming bowls and oversized fruity punches under neon.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a show-off resort punch, juicy and theatrical (a flame is welcome), but still made with fresh juice.
taglineWords: with all the neon of the Strip

concepts.reading: Southern California is sunshine citrus (navel oranges, Meyer lemons), surf culture and a long tiki coastline (San Diego's Bali Hai and Kona Kai, Martin Cate's False Idol).
concepts.guidance: Read it as bright orange-and-lemon with gold rum or tequila, easygoing and sunny.

concepts.reading: The Pacific Northwest is rain, coffee and wild blackberries, and a serious tiki scene (Portland's Hale Pele).
concepts.guidance: Read it as a dark-rum sour with blackberry or a coffee note, honey and lime: something to drink while it drizzles.

concepts.reading: New York led the craft tiki wave: Painkiller/PKNY (2009), Lani Kai (2010, where Ivy Mix's Tia Mia began), Death & Co's tropical drinks and later Sunken Harbor Club. Trader Vic's at the Plaza ran for decades before that.
concepts.guidance: Read it as modern craft tiki: high-ester rum, split bases, amaro or Campari accents and saline, made precisely.
taglineWords: for a sweaty August night in the city

concepts.reading: Chicago has deep tiki roots (a Don the Beachcomber from 1940, Trader Vic's in the Palmer House) and a modern scene with Three Dots and a Dash (2013) and Lost Lake (2015). Its winters are brutal.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a warming Beachcomber sour: aged agricole or Demerara rum, honey, allspice and falernum.
taglineWords: for when the Hawk blows off the lake

concepts.reading: London is the Royal Navy's rum ration (abolished on 'Black Tot Day', 31 July 1970), London dry gin and the 18th-century punch houses. Its tiki revival included Trailer Happiness (2003).
concepts.guidance: Read it as navy rum and gin with lime or lemon, a grog or punch with tea and bitters.
taglineWords: with a nod to Black Tot Day

concepts.reading: Paris gives absinthe (the Belle Époque 'green fairy'), Cognac, Champagne and orgeat, which is a French name. Harry's New York Bar is a cocktail landmark, and Pigalle has modern tiki bars (Dirty Dick).
concepts.guidance: Read it as Cognac or aged agricole with orgeat and citrus, a rinse of absinthe and maybe a Champagne top.
taglineWords: with a little Pigalle in it

concepts.reading: Cairo gave tiki the Suffering Bastard: Joe Scialom made it at the Shepheard's Hotel Long Bar in 1942 as a hangover cure for British officers (gin, brandy, lime, bitters and ginger beer).
concepts.guidance: Read it as a gin-and-brandy buck, dry and bracing, built long over ice.
taglineWords: for a hot afternoon on the Nile

concepts.reading: Moroccan mint tea (green gunpowder tea, fresh spearmint, plenty of sugar, poured from a height) and orange blossom water define the flavor.
concepts.guidance: Green tea isn't in the pantry, so black tea stands in, lightly. Read it as a minty tea cooler with orange-flower water and honey, long and refreshing.
taglineWords: poured from a height like Moroccan mint tea

concepts.reading: The Mediterranean summer is aperitivo: lemons, bitter orange (Campari, Aperol), vermouth, basil and sparkling wine.
concepts.guidance: Read it as bitter tiki's sunnier cousin: an Aperol or Campari spritz-sour with lemon, light rum and maybe basil.

concepts.reading: Scandinavia brings aquavit (caraway and dill; Norway's Linie is aged in sherry casks that cross the equator twice by ship), Denmark's Cherry Heering (Copenhagen, 1818) and Swedish punsch.
concepts.guidance: Lingonberry, cloudberry and cardamom are Nordic but missing from the pantry. Read it as an aquavit sour or Mai Tai riff with cherry or honey.
taglineWords: with a little fjord in it

concepts.reading: Sweden's punsch is Batavia arrack with sugar, tea and spice, born of the Swedish East India Company's arrack trade (from 1733). Traditionally it is served warm with Thursday pea soup, or chilled.
concepts.guidance: Read it as an arrack-and-punsch sour, tea-tinged and gently funky.
taglineWords: from the Swedish East India trade

concepts.reading: Scotland brings peat smoke (Islay), heather honey and Drambuie.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a smoky honey-and-citrus sour (the Penicillin is the modern template) with ginger, or a Scotch-and-rum split in a Beachcomber-style honey sour.

concepts.reading: Bali Ha'i is the imaginary island of Michener's Tales of the South Pacific (1947) and the 1949 musical. Its name went on to restaurants in San Diego, New Orleans and Hawaii.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a dreamy, lush resort punch: passion fruit, pineapple, orgeat and gold rum, with a splash of bubbles.

concepts.reading: Atlantis (and the tiki-adjacent lost continents of Lemuria and Mu) means deep blue-green water, sunken treasure and mystery.
concepts.guidance: Avoid amber or red ingredients, which turn it murky. Read it as a deep teal drink: blue curaçao with clear partners and only a little pineapple, made dry with lemon and a pinch of sea salt.

concepts.reading: Shangri-La, the hidden paradise of Lost Horizon (1933), and Eden mean a serene, lush, perfumed escape.
concepts.guidance: Read it as floral and gentle: lychee, elderflower, orange blossom and tea over light rum, softly sweet, never boozy.

concepts.reading: Before cocktails there was punch: arrack or rum, citrus, sugar, water and nutmeg, often with tea, ladled from a bowl, and the Navy's grog of rum, water and lime.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a strong, simple punch or grog: navy rum or arrack, lemon or lime, demerara, tea and nutmeg.
taglineWords: ladled before cocktails had a name

concepts.reading: The gaslight era of Jerry Thomas (1862) drank punches, sours, fixes, cobblers (the sherry cobbler was a sensation) and juleps, sweetened with raspberry or pineapple-gum syrup and curaçao.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a fruit-syrup punch or sour of brandy or Jamaican rum, with sherry and nutmeg.

concepts.reading: U.S. Prohibition (1920–1933) sent drinkers to Havana and brought rum in from 'Rum Row', the ships that waited off the coast loaded from the Bahamas, Bermuda and Cuba. At home, honey, citrus and grenadine masked rough spirits.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a sharp Daiquiri-style sour, rum or gin with lime or lemon and honey, served up.

concepts.reading: The Jazz Age means champagne and gin, Havana weekends and Paris bars.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a sparkling, citrusy sour: gin or light rum, lemon and a liqueur accent, topped with Champagne and served in a coupe.

concepts.reading: The 1930s are tiki's birth: Donn Beach opened in Hollywood as Prohibition ended and served the Zombie (1934), the Sumatra Kula and the Beachcomber's Gold to film people. His method was two or three complementary rums, fresh lime and grapefruit, secret mixes (Don's Mix, falernum, honey) and drops of anise and bitters, often flash-blended.
concepts.guidance: Read it as Don's house style.
taglineWords: the way Donn mixed them for the studio crowd

concepts.reading: In the 1940s whiskey was scarce and rum plentiful, so rum drinks boomed: the Navy Grog (c. 1941), the Mai Tai (1944), the Suffering Bastard (1942) and Pat O'Brien's Hurricane. 'Rum and Coca-Cola' topped the charts in 1945.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a rum-forward grog or sour with grapefruit and honey, or a passion-fruit punch.
taglineWords: with a swing band playing somewhere

concepts.reading: Polynesian Pop (c. 1950–1970) was tiki as mass culture: the Mai-Kai (1956), the Kahiki (1961), Steve Crane's Kon-Tiki chain, A-frame palaces, Exotica records, house mugs, bowls for the table and flaming garnishes. The drinks are the golden-age canon at its most theatrical.
concepts.guidance: Read it as layered rums, passion fruit, orgeat and falernum, served in a mug with an orchid.
taglineWords: with Martin Denny’s bird calls in the background

concepts.reading: The jet and space age gave tiki the Jet Pilot (the Luau, 1958), the Test Pilot and the Saturn (1967): gin, passion fruit, falernum, orgeat and lemon, now served in a ringed 'Saturn' glass by revival bars.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a sleek, spiced passion-fruit sour, perhaps gin-based, perhaps with a 151 kick.

concepts.reading: The 1970s were tiki's resort-and-blender decade: the frozen Piña Colada, the Tequila Sunrise (made famous by the Rolling Stones' 1972 tour), Galliano's Harvey Wallbanger, the Blue Hawaii, the Rum Runner (1972) and the Bahama Mama. Then came sweet-and-sour mix and the 'umbrella drink' reputation.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a frozen or fruity resort drink made the right way: fresh pineapple, coconut, orange and real acid.
taglineWords: made the way the 1970s should have made it

concepts.reading: The 1980s were tiki's low point and neon peak: Midori Sours, Sex on the Beach, Fuzzy Navels, coconut rum, Blue Lagoons and the Miami Vice.
concepts.guidance: Read it as bright and fruity (melon, peach, coconut, cranberry, blue), but rescued with fresh lime and real balance.

concepts.reading: The 1990s revival began with collectors and musicians, not bartenders: exotica reissues, thrift-store mugs, Sven Kirsten's research and Beachbum Berry's Grog Log (1998).
concepts.guidance: Read it as a faithful golden-age tiki sour rediscovered: aged rums, lime, honey, falernum and pineapple, in a vintage mug.
taglineWords: dug out of a thrift-store mug

concepts.reading: The 2000s revival restored the real recipes. Jeff Berry decoded the 1934 Zombie and Don's Mix (Sippin' Safari, 2007), the original Mai Tai came back, and Smuggler's Cove (2009), PKNY and the Chartreuse Swizzle (2003) made tiki a craft discipline.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a faithful, complex Beachcomber recipe: layered rums, Don's Mix, falernum, allspice and fresh citrus.
taglineWords: decoded from a dead bartender’s notebook

concepts.reading: 2010s craft tiki brought bitter tiki (Jungle Bird, Trinidad Sour), split bases (mezcal, aquavit, amaro with rum), saline, Smuggler's Cove's rum categories and bars like Lost Lake and Three Dots and a Dash.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a precise, bitter-edged, funk-forward drink with a surprising base split.

concepts.reading: Today's 'tropical' reframing centers Caribbean rum culture over Polynesian kitsch (as in Garret Richard and Ben Rojo's Tropical Standard). It favors fresh technique, clarified juices, highballs, lower ABV and zero-proof options.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a bright, clean, rum-forward tropical drink, light on décor and heavy on craft.

concepts.reading: Summer drinks are long, cold, tart and lower in alcohol: crushed ice, swizzles, coolers and punches, with mint, cucumber, watermelon, pineapple and passion fruit.
concepts.guidance: Skip the butter, cream and baking spice.
taglineWords: for the long days of summer

concepts.reading: Late summer is stone-fruit and blackberry season: peaches, apricots, the last watermelon and bramble fruit. The days are still hot but the evenings are drawing in.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a peach-and-apricot rum punch or swizzle with lemon and honey.
taglineWords: for the last warm week of summer

concepts.reading: Autumn turns tiki toward apple (cider, applejack), maple, cinnamon, allspice and aged rum or bourbon, with pomegranate and cranberry coming into season. It is still a sour or punch, not dessert.
concepts.guidance: Avoid summer-only melon, cucumber and blue liqueur.

concepts.reading: Hurricane season calls for the Hurricane itself: Pat O'Brien's 1940s original was 4 oz of dark rum with lemon and passion-fruit syrup (Fassionola, a red tropical syrup, is often cited as the early sweetener) in a hurricane-lamp glass. It's a strong, tart passion-fruit punch. Fresh lemon and real passion fruit, not neon mix.
The tropical dry season is bright sun, steady trade winds and cane-harvest time.
concepts.guidance: Read it as dry, crisp and lime-sharp: a Daiquiri or swizzle with light or cane-juice rum and grapefruit, low in sugar.

concepts.reading: Humidity calls for lift: effervescence, sharp citrus, ginger and mint, built long over plenty of ice.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a cooler or buck, dry rather than syrupy.

concepts.reading: A typhoon is the Pacific's hurricane, and tiki answered it with big group drinks like the Samoan Typhoon (Tampa): several rums, honey, lime, passion fruit, pineapple and orange.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a strong, multi-rum punch, maybe sized for sharing.
taglineWords: strong enough to be named like a storm

concepts.reading: The monsoon belongs to South and Southeast Asia: the smell of first rain (petrichor), the end of mango season, chai, ginger and fried snacks under an awning.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a gingery tea-and-spice rum punch with mango.
taglineWords: for the smell of the first monsoon rain

concepts.reading: Fog means the Fog Cutter: Trader Vic's rum, brandy and gin with lemon, orange and orgeat, finished with a sherry float ('Fog Cutter, hell. After two of these, you won't even see the stuff'). Orgeat and juice also make the drink cloudy.
Ski lodges of the 1950s warmed their guests with Hot Buttered Rum and Tom and Jerry. Snow calls for something steaming in a mug, with nutmeg on top.
taglineWords: for being snowed in, dreaming of islands

concepts.reading: Bitter cold wants warmth from the inside: a strong stirred rum old fashioned (Demerara and Jamaican rum, demerara syrup, falernum, allspice and bitters) or a hot drink. High proof, rich, spiced, and no long fizzy coolers.
taglineWords: to warm you from the inside

concepts.reading: Trade winds and sea breezes read as light and moving: crisp citrus, a little effervescence and grapefruit, in a swizzle or cooler that tastes like air off the water.
taglineWords: carried in on the trade winds

concepts.reading: Sunshine in a glass is gold: pineapple, passion fruit and gold rum with bright lime, cloudy and glowing.
concepts.guidance: Read it as cheerful, fruity and golden, not heavy.

concepts.reading: A grey day wants comfort and brightness: honey, ginger and lemon (toddy logic) over aged rum, with a whisper of allspice. Warm it if it's cold out.
The doldrums are the windless, sweltering calms near the equator where sailing ships sat for days.
concepts.guidance: Read it as slow, mellow and lazy: a gentle coconut-pineapple sipper, low in alcohol.
taglineWords: for when the wind won’t blow

concepts.reading: Lightning and 'electric' read as a jolt: fiery fresh ginger, sharp lime, a flicker of chili, effervescence and overproof white rum.
concepts.guidance: The real 'electric' garnish, the buzz button (Szechuan button) flower, isn't in the pantry.

concepts.reading: The original Tequila Sunrise, traced to the Arizona Biltmore in the 1930s, used crème de cassis; the 1970s version used orange juice and grenadine. A sunrise is a gradient: grenadine poured last sinks, so the glass shades from red at the bottom to gold at the top.
taglineWords: with the sunrise sunk to the bottom of the glass

concepts.reading: Noon is the sun overhead and the heat at its peak: crisp, tart, long and low in alcohol. A swizzle, a cooler or a Daiquiri with grapefruit, and nothing heavy or creamy.
taglineWords: for when the sun is straight overhead

concepts.reading: An afternoon is unhurried: something gentle, to sip while the light moves across the room.
taglineWords: for a long afternoon in the shade

concepts.reading: Golden hour is warm, low, gilded light, and the aperitif moment: a gold-colored drink of passion fruit, pineapple and gold or Barbados rum with lime, a light bitter edge (Aperol) or a splash of bubbles. A 'sundowner' is the drink taken as the sun drops.

Twilight and the 'violet hour' are dusky blue going violet. Butterfly-pea tea does it literally, turning from blue to violet as lemon goes in. Crème de violette or blackberry add a floral-berry note over gin or light rum.
concepts.guidance: Keep yellow juices and amber rums out, because they turn purple to brown.

concepts.reading: After dark, the torches are lit and tiki gets serious: a richer, stronger Beachcomber sour or Mai Tai with aged rums, falernum and bitters, in a mug.
taglineWords: for after the torches are lit

concepts.reading: Midnight is dark and strong: a stirred black-rum old fashioned or a dark Zombie-style showpiece with Demerara, coffee or cacao and bitters, the color of a moonless sea. Not fruity-light.
The ocean tastes of salt, not blue dye. Blue color only if blue is asked for.
concepts.guidance: Read it as saline, sharp citrus and a seafarer's rum (navy or light), with grapefruit and maybe a dry sherry note.
taglineWords: with salt spray on the rim

concepts.reading: The deep is dark, mysterious and a little dangerous: black rum and Demerara, a saline edge, falernum and a drop of anise.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a dark, strong, briny-spiced drink.

concepts.reading: A lagoon is calm, clear turquoise over white sand. For the color: about ½ oz blue curaçao with white rum, lime and coconut water, and only a little pineapple (more yellow turns it green). The flavor stays light, coconut-and-lime. Amber rums, grenadine, orange juice and bitters will make it murky.
taglineWords: clear as a lagoon at noon

concepts.reading: A coral reef is all color: coral pink, fish-bright orange and blue water.
concepts.guidance: Read it as coral-pink guava and passion fruit over light and navy rum, with banana and a pinch of salt (Fort Lauderdale's Reef Juice is the resort precedent).

concepts.reading: Surf means after the session: thirsty, salty and sunburnt.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a long, refreshing cooler with lime, pineapple, coconut water and a pinch of salt over light and Jamaican rum.
taglineWords: for after the last set of the day

concepts.reading: The castaway has a coconut and a bottle of rum.
concepts.guidance: Read it as coconut-forward (coconut water and coconut milk), aged rum and lime, served in the coconut itself: simple, rustic and resourceful.
taglineWords: for a castaway with one coconut and one bottle

concepts.reading: A harbor is the rum trade's front door: barrels on the quay, sailors ashore and grog shops.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a navy-rum grog with lime, grapefruit, honey and a splash of soda.
taglineWords: from a barrel rolled off the quay

concepts.reading: A waterfall or river is cold, clear and clean: white rum or cane rhum, lime, cucumber, mint and coconut water with soda, long and very light, nearly colorless.
A cave or hidden cove is a smuggler's hideout: dark rum, earthy and mineral, candlelit.
concepts.guidance: Read it as Demerara and pot-still rum with honey, a little salt and nutty sherry, stirred or as a dark grog.

concepts.reading: The jungle in tiki belongs to the Jungle Bird, born at the Kuala Lumpur Hilton's Aviary Bar in 1973.
A rainforest is lush, green, wet and perfumed rather than menacing. It comes out pale green from the herbs and Chartreuse.
concepts.guidance: Read it as herbaceous and grassy: cane-juice rum or cachaça, mint, green Chartreuse and passion fruit, swizzled cold.
taglineWords: lush as a cloud forest after rain

concepts.reading: The bayou and mangrove swamp are murky green and herbal. Swamp Water (reportedly a 1970s Chartreuse promotion: green Chartreuse, pineapple, lime) is the precedent, and Louisiana adds Herbsaint and Peychaud's.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a Chartreuse-pineapple swizzle with anise.

concepts.reading: The desert is agave and smoke (the Sonoran and Mexican deserts), mesquite, chili, grapefruit and salt, and it is dry. (Shannon Mustipher's Death Valley at Sunset adds papaya and ancho.)
concepts.guidance: Prickly pear and dates would be ideal but aren't in the pantry (red pitaya can stand in for prickly pear's magenta). Read it as a dry agave or mezcal sour with grapefruit, lime and a pinch of salt.

concepts.reading: An oasis is cool water and shade after the dunes: mint, cucumber, citrus, pomegranate and orange blossom.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a long, cooling, floral-minty highball.

concepts.reading: Mountains mean alpine herbal liqueurs (Chartreuse is made by monks in the French Alps), honey, gentian bitterness and thin, clean air.
concepts.guidance: Pine, génépi and kirsch would be truer but aren't in the pantry. Read it as a crisp herbal sour or swizzle with yellow or green Chartreuse, honey and lemon.

concepts.reading: A volcano is tiki's great piece of theater: the Volcano Bowl with a crater of flaming overproof rum at its center, a red-orange punch around it, and cinnamon sprinkled over the flame for sparks. The flavor is smoky (Demerara 151), passion fruit, orange and cinnamon. Safety: a little 151 in a spent lime shell, never poured from the bottle near a flame, and the flame put out before anyone drinks.
taglineWords: with a crater of fire at its heart

concepts.reading: A cane field is fresh-cut green sugarcane, grassy and vegetal. Note 'candy cane' is something else.
concepts.guidance: Read it as cane-juice spirits (rhum agricole blanc, cachaça) with lime and cane syrup (sirop de canne), Ti' Punch style or swizzled.

concepts.reading: Palm trees mean coconuts: coconut water and a little coconut cream over light or Barbados rum with lime and pineapple, served in the coconut.
A temperate forest is earthy, resinous and woody: aged spirits, maple, herbal liqueur and bitters, stirred.
concepts.guidance: Pine and fir liqueurs would be the truest note but aren't in the pantry, so this leans on rye, Chartreuse and maple.
taglineWords: with the smell of a forest floor

concepts.reading: Bamboo means light, dry and elegant: the classic Bamboo cocktail (dry sherry and dry vermouth with bitters, usually credited to Louis Eppinger at Yokohama's Grand Hotel around the 1890s), and the bamboo-walled tiki bar.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a low-alcohol, stirred sherry drink with a nutty-saline dryness.
taglineWords: light and dry as a bamboo grove

concepts.reading: Arctic and glacier mean crisp, clear and bitingly cold: white rum or aquavit, lime, mint and a little falernum, nearly colorless, shaken or swizzled very cold. The flavor is cold and clean, not hot or spiced.
Tropical flowers read as perfume: orange blossom, lychee, elderflower and honey, with Gardenia Mix (Don's butter-honey-spice batter, named for the flower) for the Pearl Diver side.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a floral, gently sweet sour garnished with an orchid.
taglineWords: with a lei’s worth of flowers

concepts.reading: Moonlight is pale and silvery-white: coconut milk, white rum, honey, falernum and lime, like the Mai-Kai's Moonkist Coconut and White Cloud. No grenadine, black rum or blue dye (a 'blue moon' is an idiom, not a color request).
concepts.guidance: Read it as soft, creamy-white and gentle.
taglineWords: pale as the moon on the water

concepts.reading: An eclipse is a bright disc blotted out: a golden passion-fruit and pineapple body with black rum floated on top so the light is eclipsed.
concepts.guidance: Float it over the back of a spoon after the body is poured over crushed ice.
taglineWords: a gold glass with its sun blotted out

concepts.reading: Polynesian navigators crossed the Pacific by the stars (the star compass), and the Southern Cross is the tropic sky's signpost. Read a starry night as a deep blue-to-violet drink with points of light: butterfly-pea tea or a little blue curaçao with clear partners, and a sparkling-wine top for the stars (its acidity nudges the pea tea violet, like a night sky). A star-anise note (five-spice) is optional.

The northern lights are green ribbons fading to violet. A pale green Chartreuse-and-lime swizzle (with a Nordic aquavit note) with blackberry liqueur sunk to the bottom gives green over violet. Butterfly-pea tea, which turns violet with citrus, can stand in for the violet band.
taglineWords: with the northern lights swizzled through it

concepts.reading: Clouds are white and airy: a silky egg-white (or coconut) foam on a pale sour of white rum, lime and orgeat. It is light in body and pale in color.
A pearl is creamy, lustrous and pale: Don the Beachcomber's Pearl Diver, made with Gardenia Mix (butter, honey and spices) and served in its own fluted glass, or a coconut-pale sour.
concepts.guidance: Read it as rich, honeyed and silky, pale gold to ivory.
taglineWords: pale and lustrous as a pearl

concepts.reading: Fire means two things in tiki: the flaming presentation (a spent lime shell with a little 151 Demerara, set alight, with cinnamon sprinkled over for sparks) and heat in the glass (cinnamon, ginger, a little chile). The drink is red-orange: passion fruit and grenadine. Safety: small amounts, never pour from the bottle near a flame, and put it out before drinking.
taglineWords: with a little fire on top

concepts.reading: Smoke comes from the spirits (mezcal's pit-roasted agave, peated Islay Scotch, the smoky wooden-still Demerara rums) and from pine-smoked lapsang souchong tea. A torched cinnamon stick or flamed orange peel adds aroma. Ivy Mix's Tia Mia (mezcal and Jamaican rum in a Mai Tai) is the craft model.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a smoky sour or stirred drink.
taglineWords: with campfire smoke curling off it

concepts.reading: Water as an element is clean, clear and flowing: very light, long and nearly colorless, with coconut water, cucumber and soda over a little white rum. Low in alcohol.

Earth reads as terroir: mezcal, rhum agricole and Haitian clairin-style cane spirits, cacao-mole bitters, Cynar, dry sherry and black tea. An earthy, savory, gently bitter drink, served in a clay cup.
taglineWords: with the taste of where it grew

concepts.reading: Air is lightness: effervescence, a fine foam and floral lift, low in alcohol.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a spritz or fizz (soda or sparkling wine, a little egg white, elderflower or yuzu).

concepts.reading: Hawaiian shave ice (with li hing mui and tropical syrups, sometimes a 'snow cap' of condensed milk), New Orleans snoballs, Mexican raspados and Filipino halo-halo all mean finely shaved ice soaked in fruit syrup.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a frozen, flash-blended fruit drink with guava, passion fruit, li hing mui and a coconut cap.
taglineWords: like Hawaiian shave ice for grown-ups

concepts.reading: Salt as the theme: a few drops of 20% saline brighten any drink without tasting salty, and a half salt rim gives real salinity. Salt flatters grapefruit, lime, agave, li hing mui and dry sherry.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a bright, citrusy, saline sour or highball.
taglineWords: with a pinch of the sea

concepts.reading: Steam means served hot: a hot buttered rum, a toddy of aged rum, honey, lemon and spice, or a hot rum punch with tea. Warming spice, no ice.
Wood means barrel age: aged rums (Barbados, Spanish-style, Jamaican), vanilla and caramel from oak, and bitters.
concepts.guidance: Read it as a stirred rum old fashioned with falernum or demerara, served in a rocks glass or barrel mug.
taglineWords: with the warmth of old oak

concepts.reading: Mineral reads as dry, saline and stony: white cane rhum with dry white wine or sherry, a little dry vermouth, saline and lime. Pale and bracing, served up.
taglineWords: dry and stony as a riverbed

concepts.reading: A truly red drink needs a red pigment that tastes good: hibiscus syrup, real-pomegranate grenadine, raspberry syrup, Campari or Cherry Heering, over a clear base (white rum, lime). Pineapple or orange juice pushes it to red-orange, cream or egg white to pink, and any blue or green muddies it to brown. A hibiscus or raspberry Daiquiri, or a Campari-edged sour, are the cleanest reds.

Deep crimson comes from dark-red ingredients: Cherry Heering, hibiscus, pomegranate juice, ruby port, sloe gin, with Campari for a brighter edge. An aged column rum keeps it deep without going brown, while too much amber Demerara or Jamaican dark turns it to mahogany.
concepts.guidance: Avoid yellow juices and cream.

concepts.reading: Pink is red diluted and clouded: grenadine, raspberry or hibiscus with egg white (a Clover Club-style foam) or coconut cream, or naturally pink guava nectar, watermelon and strawberry. Peychaud's on an egg-white sour turns it pink too. Mango and orange push it to coral.
concepts.guidance: Keep dark rums, blue and green out.

concepts.reading: Vivid magenta comes from red dragon fruit (pitaya) purée, whose betalain pigment is almost fluorescent, from hibiscus syrup (anthocyanins that stay magenta-red in acid) and from raspberry syrup. Over a clear base with lime it's electric. Cream or yellow juice would dull it.

Coral, salmon and peach (pink-orange) come naturally from guava nectar, papaya, passion fruit with a touch of grenadine, grapefruit with grenadine, or Aperol with pineapple. It's a gentle, very tropical palette that is easy to drink.

Orange comes from orange juice (cloudy), passion fruit and mango (yellow-orange), papaya and apricot, Aperol (clear and vivid) and a little grenadine for depth. Hurricane and sunset punches live here. Rust and terracotta mean adding amber rum or Campari.

Amber, copper and mahogany are the colors of aged rum: Barbados, Spanish-style and Jamaican rums with demerara syrup, Angostura, allspice dram and falernum, with no cloudy juice to hide them. Stirred drinks and rich sours with lime glow amber. Blue, red and cream all fight it.

Gold comes from pineapple juice (cloudy gold), passion fruit, honey, gold or Barbados rum, banana liqueur, and a touch of Galliano or yellow Chartreuse. A gold drink is fruity-tropical and glowing. Red pigments turn it orange, blue turns it green, and black rum browns it.
Yellow is a paler, brighter gold: pineapple juice, lemon, passion fruit, banana liqueur, Galliano and yellow Chartreuse over white rum, often with an egg-white or pineapple froth.
concepts.guidance: Keep it away from red, blue and dark rum.

concepts.reading: Green comes from green Chartreuse: herbal, bright and lime-sharp, the color of the canopy.

Pale jade is green made milky: blended fresh mint with pineapple (the Missionary's Downfall, also with peach and honey), green Chartreuse with pineapple (the Chartreuse Swizzle), or cucumber with an egg-white foam. Soft, cool and herbal.

Vivid green means melon liqueur (Midori, launched in the US in 1978) or blue curaçao with pineapple. Both are sweet, so use generous fresh lime (a proper Midori Sour), or green Chartreuse for a deeper, herbal emerald. Neon green should still taste balanced.
Harry Yee found the ocean's teal in 1957: blue curaçao with a little pineapple. This one is turquoise, clear enough to see through.
concepts.guidance: resort photos look bluer because they use more curaçao; uncertain At the classic 3 oz of pineapple the color model gives sea-green.

concepts.reading: A true blue comes from blue curaçao with clear partners, so it stays blue in the glass.
concepts.guidance: or butterfly-pea tea, which isn't in the pantry

concepts.reading: Pastel blue is blue curaçao made opaque with coconut cream or milk (or an egg-white foam): a creamy, pale-sky colada with very little yellow juice. White rum, lime, coconut and a whisper of orange.
